1:
The date is exact, and Gill counts the interval to the day from the prophet's call and his last oracle. Henry contrasts the occasion with an earlier discourse: that one answered presumptuous reflections, this hypocritical enquiries, and thinks the precision deliberate, so captives might keep count and see the years creeping toward release. Wesley notes how little time was left before the siege and suspects the delegation had settled beforehand what it meant to do. Ellicott observes that the question is never asked, and that the answer meets an unspoken concern for the nation, not a private matter. Calvin insists this is plain history, not vision, and contrasts the one channel appointed for this people with the many the nations used, soothsayers and augurs and astrologers.

Keil and Delitzsch state the plan as a historical survey: rebellion in Egypt, rebellion in the desert through both generations, forbearance only for the divine name's sake, so that a people still idolatrous at home could not expect to be consulted. Clarke gives the same outline and adds that the last five verses belong with the next chapter.

The refusal is blunt. Clarke renders it a refusal to hear or have anything to do with them. Ellicott quotes Jerome: to those who ask rightly the answer comes before the asking ends, while to men like these there is no answer but a rebuke, reinforced by an oath. Calvin reports the construction that takes the same verb in two senses, enquiring then answering, and rejects it as strained. On the question following, Ellicott makes the doubled form an imperative and judging mean preferring charges; Gill settles on reproof; Calvin holds such men are to be dismissed rather than argued with, since the Spirit does not always strive; Clarke and Wesley say the indictment must run back to the fathers, whose deeds these men approve and outdo.

The election is stated before the history. Clarke observes that the choice ran one way only, and explains the lifted hand as the gesture of an oath, a right hand raised to heaven, which lights up the psalm about a right hand of falsehood and survives in his own country's courts; Wesley prefers an arm made bare for deliverance. Henry finds the shape of the whole Bible in the sequence, a creature's rebellion following at once on his making, and calls this nation a representation of mankind both in its dealings with God and his with it.

Egypt is the awkward part of the record, and the commentators know it. Ellicott admits that neither the command against idolatry nor the rebellion against it is preserved in the law, and argues both implied — by the covenant the mission rested on, and by an order to go out and sacrifice that assumes a neglected duty; he suspects the incidents happened while the people were near enough for Egypt to hear of them. Clarke notes flatly that this is a circumstance the lawgiver did not mention. Calvin turns it the other way: the exhortation to hope had been given and a witness of the deliverance stood among them, so ingratitude had no cover.

The land promised draws comment. Clarke pictures a father surveying countries to find his children a home, and takes milk and honey for a land yielding necessities without hard labour; Wesley calls the phrase proverbial and the searching a way of speaking after the manner of men; Ellicott concedes how strange the title of glory looks after centuries of misrule, and insists it answered expectation at the entry. Then the reason for restraint. Gill and Wesley put it as honour rather than merit; Clarke and Ellicott agree that destruction would have let the nations conclude the promises broken by caprice or unkeepable; Calvin states it hardest, that the sparing came of regard for a name that would else be a laughing-stock, not of pity.
10:
Ellicott marks a second period here, the earlier wilderness years: the departure, the law, the tabernacle, the priesthood and the march to the border, by which the nation was constituted as distinctly as it ever would be. Clarke adds a detail that undercuts their credit, that they had to be forced out of a bondage they were unwilling to leave. Calvin presses the motive: the cause of the deliverance was the divine glory, and any other account the people gave was false. Henry frames the passage as a struggle between sins working to ruin a nation and mercies working to save it, and notes that the wilderness story is held up later as a warning to Christian readers.

The law is described as a gift. Clarke says it showed men what to do to be safe and wise and what to avoid so as not to be hurt in body, mind or property, so that heeding it would have made them holy, healthy and happy. Calvin adds a comparison: deliverance alone would have been inestimable, but ruling them familiarly by doctrine so they should not stray was a further generosity, and the promise attached was freely added where bare command would have served. Ellicott guards against a misreading — what was asked was never a perfunctory keeping of precepts but obedience from the heart — while allowing the older covenant rightly called one of works, the people not being educated far enough for anything else.

The sabbaths provoke the sharpest note. Clarke calls the observance the first statute given to men and a token of three things, the creation behind, the rest in the land ahead, the inheritance beyond. Ellicott points out that the institution, like circumcision, was older than this period and here re-commanded as the covenant's special pledge, and remarks how much stress the older Scriptures lay on it. Calvin faces the awkwardness: set beside the commandments forbidding strange gods, images and misuse of the name, the fourth looks lightest, and he explains its prominence by saying one precept is singled out to make the whole plainer. Wesley reduces it to a badge of belonging.

The rebellion is aggravated by its setting. Gill dwells on a place where the people were wholly dependent and kept alive daily by miracle, and notes it was the whole house and for forty years; Wesley says preserving life against beasts and barrenness was a continued miracle. Clarke observes that they behaved in the desert as in Egypt and were spared for the same reason. Calvin holds that the sons proved like their fathers, and that after the law was published no excuse remained for keeping the old affections.

The excluding oath is a middle course: Clarke says they were disinherited rather than destroyed. Ellicott specifies the sentence, everyone over twenty at the departure doomed to die outside, and insists mercy was not wholly withdrawn since the children were promised entry; Wesley states the exchange in a line. Calvin draws their character from the failed threat: fools are corrected by punishment, and men who grow worse under it are desperate. He notes that the law makes the cause a wish to turn back after a false report while the prophet assigns superstition, and holds both fit, since obedient men would never have refused to break camp.

Why the sentence stopped short returns as the chapter's refrain. Gill lists what the nations would have said had the people died in the desert — that the promiser lacked power, faithfulness or goodness, or that no such land existed — and concludes that the divine glory outweighs every other consideration. Calvin insists the restraint was no indulgence feeding their corruption: the hand was withdrawn from a just destruction, and their memory preserved. Gill adds the arithmetic that makes the mercy visible, a generation dying but for two men and another raised in their room.
18:
Ellicott opens a third section, the generation grown up in the free air of the desert under the institutions given at the mountain, while warning that the discourse is not confined to one generation: national characteristics are being described wherever they appear. Gill takes the address for the exhortations delivered on the plains before the crossing; Clarke says these children were chosen in their fathers' stead, to receive what disobedience had cost the others. Calvin hears something bleaker in the change of audience: the fathers were passed over as deaf, so that speaking to their sons was itself a verdict on them.

The charge to the sons is put as a contest of lawgivers. Calvin reads the declaration of who God is as claiming what men usurp: they will not openly strip him of authority, but set up as his partners and infect his law with their own commentary, as though it were not complete wisdom by itself. On the sabbaths, repeated a second time, he insists that bare rest was never the point, the inward sanctifying being always the end; Gill glosses hallowing as abstaining from business and attending religious duty, Wesley as remembering to keep the day holy.

The sons proved no better. Gill dates their fall to the plains of Moab and the worship joined there before the crossing; Ellicott notes that the earlier books supply illustrations in abundance. Calvin observes that both methods failed, the command pressed and the promise held out softly, and neither taking. Clarke pictures the hand raised to crush and drawn back, Wesley the posture of one about to strike who withdraws to spare.

Ellicott denies that the oath of scattering was meant for that generation. The threat is given repeatedly in the law to the nation as a whole, to be executed only when a long course of obstinacy made it unavoidable; by the prophet's own day it was partly realised and about to be completed.

Then the hardest sentence in the chapter, and all of them feel it. Clarke loses patience with the noise the verse has made among believers and unbelievers alike, and denies that God ever gave any people such statutes in the sense the words seem to bear. Ellicott argues it out: these cannot be the ordinances already described as ones a man lives by, so they are no part of the law, whatever many fathers supposed, and it will not do to say that what was given was good in itself and only turned bad in the using. Gill rejects the moral law as holy and just, notes that a law may be good to the keeper and deadly to the breaker, and inclines to ceremonial rites not good in their own nature. Calvin makes it a judicial handing over: men who refused to be governed by the doctrine of the law were left to bear another yoke. Wesley states the same in a phrase, not enjoined but permitted, and pernicious to those who used them.

The instance that follows fixes the sense. Clarke and Wesley make the polluting a permission rather than a command, Clarke insisting the practice named was one God everywhere denounced. Ellicott notes that the word for fire is supplied from a later verse, identifies the custom as consecration to Moloch, forbidden in the law, and observes that it persisted into the monarchy's last days. Calvin explains why the point was added: the people would have objected that they had not abandoned the worship of God, since they mixed the legal ceremonies with heathen inventions and thought that discharged the duty. Wesley closes on the purpose, that men who would not have him a gracious king in governing them should be made to own him a mighty one in punishing.
27:
Ellicott opens the fourth period and remarks that the longest stretch of history gets the briefest treatment, the whole settlement from conquest to the prophet's own day compressed into three verses and charged with one offence, altars on every height. Henry sharpens it: what makes this blasphemy is that the fathers had watched where the same conduct led and repeated it, and warning wasted is worse than warning never given. Calvin says the insult was intolerable because it came after possession was granted, and because the desert years had taught them nothing.

Calvin explains why hills and leafy trees were the trouble. One altar in one place was the rule, and before the nation had a fixed station even that was to be unshaped, a mound of turf or rough stone; so a landscape of high ground and thick shade was a standing invitation to do otherwise. Gill sets the ingratitude against what the entry had cost, so many difficulties passed and so much power and truth displayed.

The question put to them is read as scorn. Clarke asks what a high place is good for, and takes its name for a mark of infamy the people went on using while they went on frequenting it. Wesley makes it a puzzle about attraction: what was found there worth leaving the appointed altar for. Ellicott explains the name as simply meaning height, and dismisses as fanciful the derivation that would make it a pun on the question itself. Calvin admits the exchange looks flat and thinks commentators have missed it: the point is not information but the removal of any plea of ignorance, since they had been cautioned repeatedly.

Then the address turns from the fathers to the men in the room. Ellicott marks the fifth and last section of the review, aimed at the prophet's contemporaries, with questions that answer themselves and are answered anyway for emphasis, so that the justice of a long-threatened judgment becomes plain. Calvin says the prophet at last attacks his questioners and turns their own language against them, defending the interrogative against two older renderings, one making the clause a flat assertion and the other a negative question, which he thinks absurd.

The refusal to be consulted comes back as a refrain. Ellicott notes that it closes the section exactly where the elders' arrival opened it. Wesley turns it into a question about standing, whether men who have forsaken and reproached him are fit to ask him counsel. Calvin finds it barely credible, a people chastised out of their appetites presenting themselves as willing to obey while nothing has changed. Clarke uses the verse to settle the earlier crux: the polluting was self-inflicted and merely permitted, which is the sense in which it could be said to be given.

What the delegation actually wanted is exposed last. Calvin reads despair reaching for a solution: hated for worshipping a God of their own and separated from everyone by the law, they judged nothing would serve them better than to give up entirely and take the manners and rites of the nations. Ellicott traces the ambition back to the original demand for a king like the nations and calls it a chief cause of the idolatrous tendency; he notes too that the Hebrew ends the chapter at the close of the promise, and thinks the English should have followed, the last five verses belonging with what comes after. Wesley spells out the programme as intermarriage, trade and religion together, taken for safety. Clarke answers flatly: the scheme cannot succeed, the people will be kept distinct whether they wish it or not, and the nations they court will despise them. Gill says only that what was contrived will come to nothing.
33:
The answer is sworn, and Gill notes the oath by the divine life marks something certain and weighty. Ellicott shows how the whole reply is built out of the exodus: the phrase about a mighty hand and stretched-out arm is the standing formula of the law for the acts that brought the people out, but where it was once joined to great judgments on their oppressors it is here joined to fury poured out on themselves, so that the same power appears first as rescue and now as discipline. Henry states what is being frustrated: a plan to dissolve into the nations, which will fail because the compliant will not be allowed to share their neighbours' prosperity.

The gathering promised is not the homecoming it sounds like. Ellicott argues that it cannot mean restoration, since it is described as an act of wrath and since its stated destination is a desert, so it must describe the handling of a scattered people: they will be separated out and refused the assimilation they wanted. Calvin explains why the point had to be made — dispersion had felt like release from jurisdiction, and men who thought themselves disinherited thought themselves also free. Gill and Wesley name the refuges, the neighbouring peoples among whom the fugitives meant to settle and, as Wesley puts it, to lurk.

Where the wilderness lies divides them. Gill offers three possibilities, Babylon itself, the inhospitable countries north and east into which many were carried, or the road home, and inclines finally to the long dispersion the nation was still living in; Wesley names the same remote regions and calls them the most horrid parts of the world. Clarke takes it of the land itself, found desolate on return, and says the dealing there will either end them or mend them. Ellicott declines to locate it at all: as the past had its probation in a desert so will the future, and since the phrase about pleading face to face is borrowed from the law and meant by sense rather than letter, looking for the place on a map is idle. Calvin sets the whole stage between rejection and reconciliation, since a release from Chaldea might have been mistaken for simple favour.

Passing under the rod is the passage's best-known figure, and all of them read it from the sheepfold. Clarke gives the rabbinic detail in full: the flock penned, the shepherd at a gap wide enough for one, a rod dipped in vermilion, and the tenth marked as it went by. Calvin insists the word is a crook and not a sceptre or a stick for beating, and takes the counting as proof of ownership, the flock numbered because it has been bought. Ellicott makes the counting an examination that reconstitutes a covenant people, Wesley a muster in which men either own the sceptre or are subdued by force, and Gill turns it toward correction that brings men to confession.

The purging that follows is the point of the muster. Ellicott observes how the design worked itself out through ordinary causes at the actual return: two generations in a prosperous country had made homes there, while the homeland lay waste and surrounded by enemies, so that the sifting happened of itself. Calvin resists reading the verb as favour, since it means to pick out or discern, and what it does is drag the hidden into the light. Gill treats rebel and transgressor as one charge stated twice, and Wesley as the stubborn simply. Clarke extends the sentence to his own day, holding that those who refuse the appointed deliverer will die in their dispersion while believers are brought home, so that both parties learn the same lesson about who is speaking.
39:
The permission to serve idols is a sentence, not a licence. Clarke uses it to close the earlier crux: this is exactly how ordinances not good could be said to be given, by leaving men to their own way. Ellicott calls it the most fearful punishment imaginable, being allowed to follow one's chosen road to the end, the standing fate of obstinacy in any age. Calvin locates the offence in mixture rather than in open apostasy: the people supposed a half worship acceptable because they still owned the true God as their redeemer, and the answer is that nothing less than the whole affection will do, since no rival is admitted. Wesley states the practical upshot, that while men are idolaters they should keep the name out of their mouths.

The mountain that follows is read at three distances. Wesley keeps it literal, the hill lower than many others but raised above them by a presence, with temple rebuilt, city repeopled and offerings required as before. Gill and Clarke both take it of the church, Gill for firmness and holiness and visibility, Clarke for a day when the true sacrifice is received and thanks brought in for a gift beyond speech. Ellicott holds the middle ground carefully: nothing here, taken alone, need mean more than the return from exile, yet the parallel with an earlier and plainly Messianic passage makes it hard to think the view stopped there, the restoration being a type of the greater thing; and he warns against forcing any single phrase into direct fulfilment. Calvin says simply that the address has turned to the elect, the remnant in which the church was to survive.

Acceptance is described in the language of sacrifice, and Calvin explains why that language is safe. The worship becomes pleasing when the men who once mixed superstitions with it have finally dropped them; the word for a sweet savour is the legal formula and does not mean that incense was agreeable in itself, but that the outward rites were a real discipline as long as the truth was kept with them, and God wished to testify palpably that he had not rejected what he himself commanded. Gill turns the same phrase to expiation and imputed righteousness, and Wesley to the praise God earns by the good he does his people.

The knowledge promised is distinguished from another kind. Calvin points out that the same formula was used earlier as a threat, since the condemned also come to know a judge by the proofs of his anger; here it carries the taste of a father's love instead. Gill lists what is learned by experience and publicly owned, covenant kept, promise performed, power and mercy together; Clarke reduces it to an acknowledgment.

The chapter's last note is self-loathing, and it is read as the condition of the mercy rather than its aftermath. Calvin insists there is no reconciliation without repentance intervening, and warns that men, the devout included, take an offered pardon greedily and bury their sins under it. Gill and Clarke both extend the shame to a rejection they see continuing, Clarke allowing the promise a limited application to the return from Babylon but placing its proper fulfilment later. Ellicott takes a narrower and more historical view: idolatry was the sin the nation was reproved for through all its earlier ages, it was cured once for all at the restoration, and whatever else the people have done since they have not gone back to it. He adds that the prophecy ends here, the Hebrew and the old versions closing the chapter at this point. Calvin gives the last word to the motive that has run through the whole survey, that the glory shows most in pity spent on the abandoned, and spent for the sake of a name rather than of any merit.
45:
Everyone agrees the chapter is broken in the wrong place. Gill notes that a fresh oracle begins here, that the following chapter is an explanation and enlargement of it, and that several editors and one Jewish commentator start a new chapter at this verse; Henry says the same, that these lines have no connection with what precedes and are expounded by what follows.

The direction given is examined word by word. Ellicott points out that the one English word south stands for three different Hebrew ones, meaning the right hand — since a speaker taking his bearings faces east — the bright or noonday quarter, and the dry country, which was an ordinary name for the lower part of Palestine; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the first the same way. Ellicott also answers the obvious objection, that the target lay nearly west of the prophet: an army from Babylon could only come at it from the north, the desert lying between, so it was approached and therefore spoken of as the south.

Setting the face is read as posture and as omen together. Gill takes it for speaking boldly and without fear, and at the same time as a token that God had set his face against the place; Henry draws only the second meaning. Clarke identifies the forest with the city, as thick with people as a wood with trees, and Wesley agrees, adding a note on the verb for prophesying: the word is to distil, so that softer speech comes first and the storm afterwards.

The fire is expounded without much dispute. Clarke reads war, with the green tree for the substantial citizens and the dry for the meanest, a flame not to be quenched until the land is ruined, and terror running the length of a country that lies north and south; Wesley matches him, flourishing and poor alike, every rank from end to end. Ellicott takes the green and dry rather of moral condition, and presses the point that a national judgment sweeps away all together, with no allowance made for those less ripe in evil; he notes too that when the phrase about faces arrives the prophet has already dropped the figure for the thing meant, as he often does. Gill and Clarke agree that the neighbours as well as the sufferers will see whose hand it is.

The protest at the end is heard two ways. Gill offers three senses for it, a plea not to be sent, a plea not to be sent in figures, or a plea against the calamity itself, and records a Greek rendering that makes it a flat refusal. Clarke turns it into an anticipation of the audience: who will believe this, when they put the evil day far off and dismiss the speaker as a maker of riddles whose meaning they need not trouble to reach, which may not even concern their own time? By such reasoning, he adds, men set aside what would have done them good. Ellicott takes the obscurity as deliberate, a device used elsewhere by the same prophet to sharpen attention for the explanation he is about to give; Wesley reports only the complaint, that he cannot be understood at all.
